title: The energy change of reactions (bond energies)

notes.definition: During a chemical reaction, energy must be supplied to break bonds in the reactants and energy is released when bonds form in the products. The overall energy change is the difference between the energy needed to break bonds and the energy released by forming bonds, and can be calculated from bond energies.
explanation: During a chemical reaction, bonds in the reactants are broken and new bonds are formed in the products. Breaking a bond needs energy to overcome the attraction between the atoms, so bond breaking is an endothermic process. When a new bond forms, energy is released, so bond making is an exothermic process. Every reaction involves both, and whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic depends on which is larger.

A bond energy is the energy needed to break one mole of a particular covalent bond, measured in kJ/mol. The same amount of energy is released when one mole of that bond is formed. Bond energies are given in the question, usually in a table. For example, H–H is about 436 kJ/mol and O=O about 498 kJ/mol.

To calculate the overall energy change, first write a balanced equation and draw displayed formulae so you can count every bond. Add up the energy needed to break all the bonds in the reactants. Then add up the energy released when all the bonds in the products are formed. Overall energy change = sum of energy needed to break bonds in reactants − sum of energy released forming bonds in products. Remember to multiply each bond energy by the number of those bonds, including the numbers in front of formulae in the equation.

In an exothermic reaction, the energy released from forming new bonds is greater than the energy needed to break existing bonds, so the overall energy change is negative. In an endothermic reaction, the energy needed to break existing bonds is greater than the energy released from forming new bonds, so the overall energy change is positive. The symbol ΔH is often used for the overall energy change of a reaction.

Values calculated from bond energies are often slightly different from values measured in experiments. This is because bond energies are average values: for example, a C–H bond in methane does not have exactly the same energy as a C–H bond in ethane. Experimental values also include energy changes from changes of state, and measurements lose energy to the surroundings.
keyFacts: Breaking bonds needs energy: it is endothermic.
Forming bonds releases energy: it is exothermic.
Bond energy is the energy needed to break one mole of a bond, in kJ/mol.
Overall energy change = bonds broken (reactants) − bonds formed (products).
Exothermic: energy released forming bonds > energy needed breaking bonds; overall change is negative.
Endothermic: energy needed breaking bonds > energy released forming bonds; overall change is positive.
Count every bond using displayed formulae and the balancing numbers in the equation.
Bond energies are average values, so calculated answers differ slightly from measured values.

equations.name: Overall energy change from bond energies
equations.formula: overall energy change = sum of energy needed to break bonds in reactants − sum of energy released forming bonds in products

workedExamples.title: Hydrogen and chlorine
workedExamples.question: Calculate the overall energy change for H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl. Bond energies (kJ/mol): H–H 436, Cl–Cl 243, H–Cl 432.
steps: Negative, so the reaction is exothermic.

workedExamples.title: Combustion of methane
workedExamples.question: Calculate the overall energy change for CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O. Bond energies (kJ/mol): C–H 413, O=O 498, C=O 805, O–H 464.
steps: Bonds broken: 4 × C–H = 4 × 413 = 1652; 2 × O=O = 2 × 498 = 996; total = 2648 kJ/mol.

workedExamples.title: Finding an unknown bond energy
workedExamples.question: For H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl the overall energy change is −185 kJ/mol. H–H = 436 kJ/mol and Cl–Cl = 243 kJ/mol. Calculate the H–Cl bond energy.
steps: Overall change = bonds broken − bonds formed, so −185 = (436 + 243) − 2x.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think breaking bonds releases energy.
misconceptions.right: In fact breaking bonds always needs energy (endothermic). Energy is released only when bonds form.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often subtract the other way round: bonds formed − bonds broken.
misconceptions.right: In fact the overall energy change is bonds broken − bonds formed, so an exothermic reaction gives a negative answer.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often forget the balancing numbers when counting bonds.
misconceptions.right: In fact 2HCl contains two H–Cl bonds and 2H₂O contains four O–H bonds; multiply by the numbers in the equation.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think a calculated value should exactly match the measured value.
misconceptions.right: In fact bond energies are averages, so calculated values are only approximate.

realWorld: Chemists use bond energy calculations to estimate how much energy fuels such as hydrogen and methane will release before testing them.
The very strong N≡N triple bond needs a lot of energy to break, which is one reason why making ammonia from nitrogen in the Haber process needs a catalyst and high temperature.
higherTier: This whole subtopic is Higher tier only.
Calculate the energy transferred in chemical reactions using bond energies supplied.
Explain that in exothermic reactions the energy released from forming new bonds is greater than the energy needed to break existing bonds, and the reverse for endothermic reactions.
examTips: Draw displayed formulae first and tick off each bond as you count it.
Write two clear totals: 'energy in (bonds broken)' and 'energy out (bonds formed)', then subtract in the order broken − formed.
Always include the sign (+ or −) and the unit kJ/mol in your final answer.
If asked to explain, use the comparison: 'more energy is released forming bonds than is needed to break bonds'.
Check that the number of each type of atom is the same on both sides before counting bonds.
summary: Bond breaking is endothermic; bond making is exothermic.
Overall energy change = bonds broken − bonds formed.
Negative answer: exothermic; positive answer: endothermic.
Count bonds carefully using displayed formulae and balancing numbers.
Bond energies are averages, so answers are approximate.

questions.question: Which statement about breaking a chemical bond is correct?
options: It releases energy, so it is exothermic
It needs energy, so it is endothermic
It needs no energy
It releases energy, so it is endothermic
markScheme: 1 mark: it needs energy, so it is endothermic
questions.explanation: Energy must be supplied to overcome the attraction between bonded atoms, so bond breaking is endothermic.

questions.question: What happens when a new chemical bond forms?
options: Energy is taken in from the surroundings
No energy change happens
The temperature of the surroundings falls
Energy is released to the surroundings
questions.explanation: Bond making is exothermic: energy is released when atoms bond together.

questions.question: Which expression gives the overall energy change of a reaction from bond energies?
options: Energy to break bonds in reactants − energy released forming bonds in products
Energy released forming bonds in products − energy to break bonds in reactants
Energy to break bonds in reactants + energy released forming bonds in products
Energy released forming bonds in products × energy to break bonds in reactants
questions.explanation: Overall energy change = bonds broken − bonds formed. Doing it the other way round gives the wrong sign.

questions.question: In an exothermic reaction, which statement is true?
options: Energy needed to break bonds is greater than energy released forming bonds
No bonds are broken
Energy released forming bonds is greater than energy needed to break bonds
Energy needed to break bonds equals energy released forming bonds
markScheme: 1 mark: energy released forming bonds is greater
questions.explanation: If more energy is released by forming new bonds than is taken in by breaking bonds, the extra energy is transferred to the surroundings.

questions.question: What is the sign of the overall energy change calculated for an exothermic reaction?
options: Positive
Negative
Zero
It can be either
questions.explanation: Bonds broken − bonds formed gives a negative number when more energy is released forming bonds than is needed to break them.

questions.question: Explain why energy is needed to break a covalent bond.
acceptedAnswers: attraction between nuclei and shared electrons
markScheme: 1 mark: to overcome the (strong) attraction between the bonded atoms / between the nuclei and the shared pair of electrons
questions.explanation: Bonded atoms are held together by strong attractions. Energy must be supplied to pull them apart.

questions.question: The reaction between hydrogen and oxygen is exothermic. Explain why, in terms of bond breaking and bond making.
markScheme: 1 mark: energy is needed to break bonds and released when bonds form
1 mark: more energy is released forming new bonds (O–H) than is needed to break existing bonds (H–H and O=O)
questions.explanation: The comparison is the key point: energy out from bond making is larger than energy in for bond breaking.

questions.question: State what is meant by the term bond energy.
acceptedAnswers: energy to break one mole of a bond
markScheme: 1 mark: the energy needed to break one mole of a particular (covalent) bond
questions.explanation: Bond energies are given per mole of bonds, in kJ/mol.

questions.question: The thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate is endothermic. Explain this in terms of the energy changes when bonds are broken and formed.
acceptedAnswers: greater than energy released forming bonds
markScheme: 1 mark: the energy needed to break bonds in the reactants
1 mark: is greater than the energy released when bonds form in the products (so the overall energy change is positive)
questions.explanation: In an endothermic reaction more energy goes in to break bonds than comes out when new bonds form, so energy is taken from the surroundings.

questions.question:
A student calculated the overall energy change for the reaction:
H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl
The student's answer was +247 kJ/mol.
Table 1 shows the bond energies the student used.
Identify the mistake the student made and give the correct answer.
markScheme: 1 mark: the student only included one H–Cl bond; two molecules of HCl form, so there are two H–Cl bonds
questions.explanation: 679 − 432 = +247, so the student forgot the 2 in front of HCl. The correct energy released is 2 × 432 = 864 kJ/mol.

questions.question: Methane burns: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O. State which bonds are broken and which bonds are formed, including how many of each.
questions.explanation: Draw displayed formulae: CH₄ has four C–H bonds, each O₂ has one O=O, CO₂ has two C=O, and each H₂O has two O–H.

questions.question: Give two reasons why the overall energy change for burning methane measured in an experiment is different from the value calculated using bond energies.
acceptedAnswers: water may be liquid not gas
markScheme: 1 mark: bond energies are average values (not exact for the bonds in these molecules)
1 mark: in the experiment energy is lost to the surroundings / the water formed may condense (change of state) / combustion may be incomplete
questions.explanation: Bond energies apply to gases and are averaged over many compounds. Real measurements include losses to the surroundings and changes of state.

questions.question: Describe the energy changes that take place when bonds are broken and formed during a chemical reaction, and explain how these changes decide whether a reaction is exothermic or endothermic.
markScheme: Indicative content: bonds in the reactants are broken; breaking bonds needs energy (is endothermic) to overcome attraction between atoms; new bonds form in the products; forming bonds releases energy (is exothermic); overall energy change = energy needed to break bonds − energy released forming bonds; if more energy is released forming bonds than is needed to break bonds, the reaction is exothermic and the overall change is negative; if more energy is needed to break bonds than is released forming bonds, the reaction is endothermic and the overall change is positive.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): clear description of bond breaking and bond making with the correct energy direction, and a correct comparison for both exothermic and endothermic reactions.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): some correct statements, for example bond breaking needs energy, with little comparison.
questions.explanation: A full answer covers both processes and then compares them. Remember that bond breaking always needs energy, and bond making always releases it.
